passage: So, you asked how I handled it when Alka said my goalkeeping was the reason we lost. Honestly? My first reaction was, "Then you get in the net." I had the words ready. But I bit my tongue and went home. That night I watched the match video my dad took. And, yeah, I was coming off my line too early. Twice. It stung. At the next practice I went up to Alka and said, "You were right about the line. Can you shout 'stay' when you see me move early?" She looked surprised and said, "Okay, Minakshi." I think she expected a fight. Now she shouts "stay" every game, and it's kind of our thing. We conceded one goal last match.

qa.q: What did Minakshi ask Alka to shout?
qa.a: "Stay," when Alka sees Minakshi move early.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling right after Alka's criticism?
qa.a: Hurt and defensive, ready to snap back with "Then you get in the net."

qa.q: What turned the criticism into something useful?
qa.a: Checking the video before reacting, then asking Alka for a specific signal, made the feedback practical instead of a fight.

qa.q: Why might Alka have looked surprised?
qa.a: She probably expected Minakshi to argue, so a calm request for help was unexpected.

grounding: It shows a teenager taking hard criticism without hostility and turning it into a cooperative fix.

passage: I'm Gopika, and I was in Vasudha's group for the science exhibition. It got ugly. Karan said, in front of everyone, that the model looked terrible and Vasudha's design was a waste of time. I expected her to cry or yell. She did neither. She took a breath and said, "Okay, what exactly looks wrong to you?" He pointed at the wiring. She looked. "That's fair. Can you help me hide it?" Then he said the colours were bad too, and she said, "That part I disagree with, but let's ask the others." We voted, and her colours stayed. I don't know how she felt inside. Her hands were a bit shaky. But by the end, Karan was helping.

qa.q: What did Karan point at when asked what looked wrong?
qa.a: The wiring.

qa.q: What might Vasudha's shaky hands suggest?
qa.a: She was probably upset or tense inside, even though she kept her voice calm.

qa.q: What made Vasudha's response diplomatic?
qa.a: She asked for specifics, accepted the fair part, disagreed calmly on the rest and let the group vote.

qa.q: How might Karan have felt when Vasudha asked him to help hide the wiring?
qa.a: Perhaps disarmed, since his point was taken seriously, which made it easier for him to join in.

grounding: It shows, from a classmate's view, a teenager receiving harsh criticism calmly and settling a group conflict diplomatically.

passage:
Monday: Usha Ma'am returned Pradeep's college essay covered in red: "Too general. Where are YOU in this?" Pradeep, seventeen, crumpled it into his bag. "She just doesn't get my style," he told his friend.
Thursday: At home he smoothed out the page and read her notes again, slowly. The line about his grandfather's tailoring shop had a small tick beside it: "More of this." He sat back. She wasn't wrong.
The next Monday: He handed her a new draft built around the tailoring shop and thanked her for being direct. "Tell me if it's still too general," he said. She smiled and picked up her pen.

qa.q: Which part of the essay did Usha Ma'am tick?
qa.a: The line about his grandfather's tailoring shop.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling on Monday when he crumpled the essay?
qa.a: Stung and defensive, blaming her for not understanding his style.

qa.q: What changed between Monday and Thursday that helped Pradeep?
qa.a: He reread the feedback calmly and looked for what was useful, like the tick, instead of reacting to the red ink.

qa.q: How might Usha Ma'am see Pradeep's thank-you and new draft?
qa.a: Pleased that her direct feedback landed well, and happy to keep helping. 😊

grounding: It shows a teenager moving from defensiveness to openly using a teacher's criticism over a week.

passage: 'Reena, you slammed your laptop shut when your coach said your essay was weak,' said Dhruv Mama. 'I did worse at your age. I was sixteen and editor of the school magazine. A teacher returned my article covered in red, and I told her, in front of everyone, that she didn't understand humour. Then I went home and sulked. My father read the red marks and said, "Half of these are right. Which half?" So I sat and sorted them. Seven were fair. Three I still disagreed with. Next day I thanked her for the seven and asked, politely, if we could discuss the three. She agreed with me on two. We ran that magazine together for two more years.'

qa.q: How many of the teacher's comments did young Dhruv decide were fair?
qa.a: Seven.

qa.q: What did young Dhruv feel when the article came back covered in red?
qa.a: He felt hurt and defensive, which is why he snapped at the teacher and sulked at home.

qa.q: What could Reena try with her coach's comments?
qa.a: She could sort them into fair and unclear ones, thank the coach for the fair ones and ask calmly about the rest.

qa.q: How might the teacher have felt when Dhruv came back politely?
qa.a: She was probably relieved and more willing to listen, since she agreed with him on two points.

grounding: Shows a teenager moving from defensiveness to sorting criticism fairly and resolving the disagreement politely.

passage: Twenty minutes before their group presented, Sonali scrolled through Chaitanya's slides in the school computer room and frowned. 'Too much text. Nobody will read this.' Chaitanya, sixteen, felt heat rise up his neck; he had stayed up till one making them. He opened his mouth, closed it, and breathed out. 'Show me which ones.' She pointed at four. Meanwhile the fourth member, who had only done the survey, muttered that it was all fine. Chaitanya didn't snap at him either. 'You know the survey numbers best. Can you explain slide six out loud instead of us reading it?' The boy nodded, surprised. With eight minutes left they cut the text to headings. Then the printer jammed, so they presented straight from the screen. It went fine.

qa.q: How long before the presentation did Sonali look at the slides?
qa.a: Twenty minutes before.

qa.q: What does the heat rising up Chaitanya's neck suggest he felt, and how did he handle it?
qa.a: He felt stung after working late, but he paused and breathed so he could listen instead of snapping.

qa.q: Which choice helped the group most, and why?
qa.a: Asking Sonali to show which slides were weak, because it turned criticism into specific fixes under time pressure.

qa.q: How might the quiet fourth member have felt when Chaitanya gave him slide six?
qa.a: Surprised and included, since he was given a real part instead of blame. 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a teenager taking blunt feedback calmly and smoothing group tension under time pressure.

passage: In the Delhi school staffroom, Manjula Ma'am handed back Rukmini's essay covered in red. "Your argument is strong, but your evidence is thin. And paragraph three repeats paragraph one." Rukmini, sixteen, felt her face burn. "I worked on this for a week." "I can see that. That's why I marked it this carefully." Rukmini wanted to argue. Instead she took a breath and looked at paragraph three. It did repeat. "Can you show me what strong evidence would look like here?" she asked. Manjula smiled and pulled up a chair. Rukmini uncapped her pen and wrote "evidence?" in the margin of every paragraph.

qa.q: What did Manjula Ma'am say about paragraph three?
qa.a: It repeats paragraph one.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when her face burned?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and defensive, hurt that her week of work was criticised.

qa.q: What worked in Rukmini's response, and why?
qa.a: Pausing to check the comment and asking for an example, because it turned criticism into learning.

qa.q: How does Manjula Ma'am see Rukmini's question?
qa.a: She seems pleased and ready to help, since Rukmini is open to feedback.

grounding: Shows a teenager receiving critical feedback without turning defensive and asking how to improve.

passage: I'm Nikita, and at seventeen I thought I was a good runner. Then Coach Bhupen watched my 800 metres and said, "Your arms cross your body. You're wasting energy." I snapped, "I came first, didn't I?" and walked off. For a week I avoided him. Then I watched a video of my race, and there it was: my arms swinging across like a windmill. I went back and said, "You were right. Can you help me fix it?" He did. My time dropped four seconds. I still hate hearing criticism, but I've learned to wait a day before I answer.

qa.q: What did Coach Bhupen say about Nikita's arms?
qa.a: The arms cross the body, wasting energy.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel when the coach first criticised her?
qa.a: Nikita felt defensive and hurt, having just won the race.

qa.q: What turning point changed Nikita's response to feedback?
qa.a: Watching the video of the race and seeing the problem for herself.

qa.q: How might Coach Bhupen have felt when Nikita came back?
qa.a: Pleased and relieved that Nikita was ready to listen and improve.

grounding: Shows a teenager learning to receive a coach's criticism without defensiveness.

passage:
Lab report feedback note, Class 11. Raghav Menon, physics teacher.
I returned Sabina's lab report with comments: good data, but the conclusion claimed more than the results show. At first she argued. "But everyone writes it like that, Sir." Her voice was tight and she was gripping the paper. I didn't argue back; I asked her to read her conclusion aloud next to the data table. She stopped halfway. After a long pause she said, "Okay. I see what you mean." Then she asked how to phrase it better. She rewrote it before the bell, much more carefully. I've told her she can bring the next report to me for a quick check before submitting.

qa.q: What did the conclusion do wrong, according to the comments?
qa.a: It claimed more than the results show.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when she gripped the paper?
qa.a: She felt defensive and upset about the criticism.

qa.q: What did Raghav Menon do that helped Sabina accept the feedback?
qa.a: He didn't argue back and instead asked her to compare her conclusion with the data herself.

qa.q: How might Raghav Menon see Sabina's change during the class?
qa.a: He likely feels pleased and encouraged that she moved from arguing to asking how to improve.

grounding: A teacher's note records a student moving from defensive to open in receiving feedback.

passage:
Wednesday. Rashmi's diary.
Charu told me my project slides were "too much text and nobody will read them." In front of the group! My face went hot and I said, "At least I actually made slides," which was mean because she did the research. Then everyone went quiet. I went to the washroom and breathed. When I came back, I asked her, "Which slides are the worst?" She showed me three. She was right. They were walls of words. I said sorry for the slide comment and she said sorry for saying it in front of everyone. We fixed them together. I still hate being corrected, but I think I'm getting better at not biting back.

qa.q: How many slides did Charu point out as the worst?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel when Charu criticised the slides in front of the group?
qa.a: Rashmi felt embarrassed and defensive, with a hot face.

qa.q: What worked in how Rashmi repaired the conflict?
qa.a: Taking a break to breathe, then asking Charu for specifics and apologising for the mean comment.

qa.q: How might Charu have felt after Rashmi's first reply?
qa.a: Charu may have felt hurt and dismissed, since she had done the research.

passage:
In the village school's science fair, Rashmi's water-filter model got the lowest mark in her group. The judge, a teacher from the block office, wrote: "Idea good. Testing weak. No data."
Rashmi's face went hot. Hemant, her partner, had built the frame and said loudly, "He doesn't understand village conditions."
Rashmi almost agreed. Instead she walked to the judge's table. "Sir, what data would you want?"
He showed her: water before and after, three samples, a simple table.
Back home she and Hemant argued behind the cowshed. "You're taking his side," he said.
"I'm taking our model's side. We didn't test it. That's true."
Hemant kicked a stone, then sighed. "Fine. You write the table. I'll collect the samples from the handpump."

qa.q: What did the judge write on Rashmi's model?
qa.a: "Idea good. Testing weak. No data."

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel when she first read the mark?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and stung; her face went hot.

qa.q: What made Rashmi's approach work with the judge and with Hemant?
qa.a: She asked the judge what data he wanted instead of arguing, and told Hemant calmly that she was on their model's side.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel about the feedback at first?
qa.a: He felt defensive and hurt, blaming the judge and accusing Rashmi of taking his side.

grounding: Shows a teen taking criticism openly and settling a partner's anger without hostility.

passage:
The Oslo youth orchestra had one rehearsal left before the spring concert. The conductor stopped the strings and said, "Lars, you rush the second bar every time."
Lars felt his jaw tighten. Sofia, sharing his music stand, whispered, "You do, a bit."
He wanted to snap that she dragged, not that he rushed. Instead he nodded. "Can we try it slower?"
They played it again. He rushed less.
At the break, Sofia said, "Sorry if I made it worse."
"You didn't," Lars said. "But next time tell me after, not while he's looking. It's easier."
She thought about it. "Fair. And you tell me when I drag."
"You drag in bar thirty," he said, and she laughed.

qa.q: Which bar did the conductor say Lars rushed?
qa.a: The second bar.

qa.q: What was Lars feeling when Sofia whispered that he did rush?
qa.a: He felt defensive and irritated; his jaw tightened and he wanted to snap back.

qa.q: What did Lars do well in handling the feedback?
qa.a: He accepted the correction, tried it again, and later calmly asked Sofia to tell him after rehearsal instead of mid-scene.

qa.q: How might Sofia have felt when Lars told her about bar thirty?
qa.a: Sofia probably felt relieved and amused that the tension had turned into fair, friendly feedback.

grounding: Shows a teen accepting criticism and settling a stand-partner conflict calmly.

passage:
At the district football academy, Coach pinned the match ratings on the board. Hemant had a five out of ten: "Lost the ball, lost your head."
Asif, the captain, read it over his shoulder. "You shouted at the ref. We got a yellow because of you."
Hemant turned. "And you never pass to me."
The changing room went still.
Hemant breathed out. "Okay. The shouting was wrong. I'll say sorry to Coach. But I'd like us to talk about passes, not now, after training."
Asif looked surprised. "Fine. After training."
Later, sitting on the bench, they watched the match video. Asif saw two times he could have passed. Hemant saw three times he had drifted offside. They wrote both on a scrap of paper and gave it to Coach.

qa.q: What rating did Hemant get?
qa.a: A five out of ten.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel when Asif blamed him for the yellow card?
qa.a: He felt hurt and angry, snapping back that Asif never passed to him.

qa.q: How did Hemant turn the argument around?
qa.a: He admitted the shouting was wrong and suggested talking about passes after training, which cooled things down.

qa.q: How might Asif see Hemant after watching the video together?
qa.a: Asif may respect Hemant more and feel less angry, having seen his own missed passes too.

grounding: Shows a teen receiving harsh feedback, owning his part and settling a conflict calmly.
